text.title: Definition Of Ready Checklist Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for definition-of-ready-checklist. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: A story is READY only when all 8 items pass: clear outcome, named acceptance criteria, design or wireframe linked, dependencies resolved, env access granted, test data identified, security/legal sign-off (if applicable), client PM accountable; less than or equal to 7/8 equals NOT READY and routes back to refinement.

rationale.source: PMBOK 7 + IIBA BABOK v3 readiness criteria

rule.rationale: Partial readiness is the expensive state: a story with 7 of 8 items looks estimable, so the team commits to it and then stalls mid-sprint on the one missing item. A binary gate pushes the cost of the gap into refinement, where it costs a conversation, instead of into the sprint, where it costs committed capacity.

rule.statement: Client-side dependency check (5 items) is mandatory and runs BEFORE engineering check: (a) client PM confirmed in writing, (b) env credentials or VPN tested by a team member, (c) realistic test dataset accessible, (d) regulator/legal/security ticket exists or is N/A in writing, (e) any required client-side IT change is ticketed with a stated SLA.
rule.rationale: Engineering readiness can be fixed by the team within hours; client-side readiness cannot, because a VPN account or a legal sign-off runs on the client's calendar, not the sprint's. Running the engineering check first spends effort on stories that were never going to start, and hides the long-lead blocker until the sprint has already begun.

rule.statement: Stories carrying compliance impact (HIPAA, GDPR, SOC2, PCI) require a named compliance contact and a written N/A or sign-off attached; without it, ready=false regardless of other items.
rule.rationale: Compliance impact is discovered late by default: nobody volunteers to own it, so the story enters the sprint on the implicit belief that someone will sign off. Forcing a named contact and a written N/A converts that belief into either a person with a deadline or an explicit record that the regime does not apply, and only those two survive an audit.

rule.statement: DoR check is timeboxed to 5 minutes per story in grooming; if the story cannot be evaluated in 5 minutes, mark NOT READY for 'insufficient definition' and route to a dedicated discovery session.
rule.rationale: Grooming has a fixed budget shared by the whole backlog. A story that cannot be assessed in five minutes is not slow because the team is careless, it is slow because the requirement is undefined, and the room will happily spend forty minutes doing discovery disguised as refinement while the rest of the backlog goes unrefined. The timebox converts that signal into a routing decision.

rule.statement: Every DoR failure is logged with the failing item id; the top failing item per client is the discovery focus for the next iteration.
rule.rationale: Without the failing item id, DoR failures register as generic client-is-slow friction and nothing changes. Logged by item, the same id recurring across stories names one broken upstream process, such as test-data provisioning or legal sign-off, and fixing that removes a whole class of future failures instead of one story's blocker.

rule.statement: Re-estimation of the same story is forbidden until the prior DoR failure has been cleared in writing; this enforces upstream work and removes the false comfort of re-estimating a blocked story.
rule.rationale: Re-estimating feels like progress and produces a number, so it substitutes for the unglamorous work of chasing the client for the missing dependency. The number is also meaningless, since nothing about the story has changed except the team's guess. Blocking re-estimation removes the only cheap activity available and leaves the real blocker as the sole way forward.

rule.statement: The checklist is co-owned by BA + PM and reviewed quarterly with the client; clients who consistently produce DoR failures get a written escalation in the QBR — DoR is the client-side accountability artefact.
rule.rationale: Client-caused delay is recorded as vendor-caused delay unless someone is counting. A BA raising it in a working session is heard as an excuse; the same data aggregated over a quarter and co-signed by BA and PM is heard as a process finding. The artefact exists to move the conversation out of the delivery channel, where it damages the relationship, into the governance channel, where it changes behaviour.

rule.statement: If the team has no client-side dependencies at all or operates entirely in-house, return `skipped` — methodology overhead does not pay back.
rule.rationale: The whole gate is built around dependencies the team cannot resolve itself. An in-house team owns its environments, data and approvals, so every item collapses into asking the person at the next desk. The checklist then adds a grooming ritual and a failure log while removing no wait states, and a team that feels that treats the entire gate as theatre.
